name: Benjamin E. Mays
paragraphs: Benjamin E. Mays was a monumental educator and civil rights leader who transformed Morehouse College and the Atlanta Board of Education into engines for social change and Black leadership. Alongside his wife and partner in community uplift, Sadie Gray Mays, his intellectual and moral legacy remains anchored in Atlanta as a definitive force in 20th-century American progress.

name: William H. Crogman
paragraphs: William H. Crogman was a distinguished educator and civic leader who served as a cornerstone of Atlanta's intellectual landscape, championing academic excellence and character development for the Black community. His visionary institutional leadership during a transformative era in the South fostered both educational progress and lasting civic growth.

name: Robert Grant
paragraphs: Courtesy of Zion Hill Baptist Church

Robert Grant was a skilled blacksmith and drayman who founded Zion Hill Baptist Church, embodying the vital intersection of labor and spiritual leadership in post-Civil War Atlanta. His life serves as a testament to the foundational role of the Black church in fostering community resilience and organizing African American life during Reconstruction.
Source: Courtesy of Zion Hill Baptist Church Archives

name: Grace Towns Hamilton
paragraphs: Grace Towns Hamilton was a pioneering civil rights leader and the first Black woman elected to the Georgia General Assembly. Throughout her career, she advocated for education reform, social justice, and equal opportunity for marginalized communities. Hamilton’s work broke racial and gender barriers in public office and created space for greater representation in Georgia politics. Her legacy represents persistence, public service, and community advocacy.

name: Alonzo Herndon
paragraphs: Alonzo Herndon rose from enslavement to become one of the wealthiest Black entrepreneurs in the United States. He founded the Atlanta Life Insurance Company, which provided financial security to Black families at a time when most white-owned companies refused to serve them. Beyond business success, Herndon invested in his community, creating jobs and supporting Black economic independence. His life story embodies resilience, innovation, and empowerment.

name: Annie L. McPheeters
paragraphs: Courtesy of Auburn Avenue Research Library

Annie L. McPheeters was one of the first African American librarians in Atlanta. She moved to the city to attend Clark Atlanta University and dedicated her career to increasing literacy and convenient access to books and historical information.

McPheeters started special programs to increase literacy and library use in the Black community. She became the first African American reference librarian at Georgia State College and worked with Black advocacy groups to help end segregation in Atlanta public libraries.

name: John W. Dobbs
paragraphs: John Wesley Dobbs was one of the most influential African American leaders in Atlanta during the mid-20th century. Born in 1882 in Kennesaw, Georgia, he rose from humble beginnings to become a powerful voice for civil rights and political participation.

Dobbs earned the honorary title 'Mayor of Auburn Avenue' for his tireless work in the Sweet Auburn community, which he helped transform into a thriving center of Black business and culture. He was a founding member of the Atlanta Civic and Political League and registered over 10,000 African American voters in Georgia.

name: Graham W. Jackson Sr.
paragraphs: Graham W. Jackson Sr. was a celebrated musician best known for playing the accordion at President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s funeral in 1945. His performance of “Going Home” became an iconic image in American history. During a time of racial segregation, Jackson’s musical talent earned him national recognition and respect. His career reflects the cultural influence and artistic excellence present within Atlanta’s Black community.
Source: Wikipedia contributors, 'Graham W. Jackson Sr.'

name: Ludie Clay Andrews
paragraphs: Ludie Clay Andrews was a pioneering medical professional who broke racial barriers in Georgia's healthcare system, serving as the first African American registered nurse in the state. Her decades of leadership at Spelman College's MacVicar Hospital laid the groundwork for future generations of Black healthcare providers in the South.

name: Bazoline E. Usher
paragraphs: Bazoline E. Usher was a trailblazing educator whose 40-year career in Atlanta Public Schools broke barriers for African American students and faculty. As the first African American to hold an office in Atlanta City Hall, she expanded opportunity and shaped the future of Black education in the segregated South.

name: John Lewis
paragraphs: John Lewis was a key leader in the Civil Rights Movement and later a longtime U.S. Representative for Georgia's 5th Congressional District. As a young activist, he served as chairman of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC) and helped organize sit-ins and voter registration efforts across the South.

In 1965, Lewis led marchers across the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma, Alabama, where he was beaten by state troopers on what became known as "Bloody Sunday." His courage helped lead to the passage of the Voting Rights Act. He went on to serve more than thirty years in Congress, continuing his advocacy for civil rights and democracy.

name: Dr. Moses Amos
paragraphs: Courtesy of Association of Black Health-System Pharmacists

Born in 1866 as a free man in Georgia, Moses Amos rose from a young apprentice to become the state’s first licensed Black pharmacist. After beginning his career under Dr. Jacob C. Huss and later managing a drugstore for Dr. Butler and Dr. Slater, Amos eventually purchased the business and renamed it the Gate City Drug Store in 1914. Over a 50-year career, he filled over a million prescriptions and became a prominent Atlanta entrepreneur known for his social impact. Beyond his commercial success, Amos was a trailblazer in workforce equity—hiring some of the city's first Black women clerks—and served as a vital mentor, training a new generation of Black medical and pharmaceutical professionals.
Source: Association of Black Health-System Pharmacists

name: Dinah Watts Pace
paragraphs: Dinah Watts Pace was born into slavery before the Civil War and gained freedom at 12 years old. She moved to Atlanta after becoming free and studied at Atlanta University to become a teacher.
In 1883, she opened a school for African-American children. The following year, she started an orphanage for African-American children and raised money to give the children a better life.
Pace opened her own school and orphanage for African-American children in Covington, GA. There is a park and a road named after her in Covington to honor her impact on the community.

name: Freddye Henderson
paragraphs: Freddye Scarborough Henderson was the first African American to study Fashion Merchandising at her school. She helped create a national group for fashion designers and held a big fashion show for African American people in 1953.

With her husband, she started a travel service company specializing in helping people take cultural trips to Africa and connect with their homeland. Freddye Scarborough Henderson opened her travel service in Atlanta. She played a huge role in impacting the lives of historical figures like Dr. MLK Jr., and even arranged the trip for him to get his Nobel Prize. She also affected the lives of everyday citizens, helping them take trips back to Africa to connect with their heritage.

name: Carolyn D. Yancey
paragraphs: Carolyn Dunbar Yancey graduated with a degree in education and social work and started her career as a public school teacher. She was featured in a Southern Belle calendar for her work in teaching.
Yancey was a member of many important groups like the NAACP and League of Women Voters, and held leadership positions in groups like the Wesley Community Center and Spelman College.
She was elected and served on the Atlanta Board of Education for 16 years. She was also appointed as the first African American woman to the Georgia University System Board of Regents.

name: Geneva Haugabrooks
paragraphs: Geneva Moton Haugabrooks moved to Atlanta to go to Spelman College. She worked as a teacher at a school in Fayette County before entering the business world.
In 1929, she started her own funeral home with less than $300, becoming the first and only Black female to open a funeral home in Atlanta at the time.

Nicknamed "Mama Haugabrooks," she was an important figure in the Atlanta community. She won awards for outstanding service in the community and worked with many groups such as the YMCA and the Urban League.
She used her education to become a teacher and then a pioneering business owner, being an inspiration to others. She loved helping others and played a major role in supporting her community.

name: Horace Mann Bond
paragraphs: Horace Mann Bond was one of the first African Americans to earn a PhD in education. He worked to improve education for Black students throughout his career.
Bond served as president of two historically Black universities — Lincoln University and Fort Valley State University — and as Dean of the School of Education at Atlanta University.

He wrote books explaining how racism affected Black students. His research helped support Brown v. Board of Education, which overturned "separate but equal" and helped start desegregation and the Civil Rights Movement.

Horace Mann Bond was a leader in Black education and dedicated his life to improving education for Black students. He believed in equal education for Black and white students. He worked as the Dean of the School of Education at Atlanta University, which is now Clark Atlanta University. He was also the father of civil rights leader and state congressman Julian Bond.

name: Jean Childs Young
paragraphs: Jean Childs Young built early childhood curriculum in Atlanta Public Schools and wrote "Bridging the Gap" (1970) for parents to better understand child development and support their learning at home.

Young helped launch Atlanta Junior College (now Atlanta Metropolitan College). She backed Dream Jamboree, SciTrek, and APEX Museum growth. Her legacy lives on through awards, scholarships, and a middle school named after her.

Jean Childs Young helped Atlanta become what it is today through education and helping the youth. She improved schools, created pathways to college, and helped celebrate and teach Black history. She supported Atlanta's Olympics with education. Her impact is seen in many scholarships, awards, and a southwest Atlanta middle school named after her. She was also the wife of former civil rights leader and Atlanta Mayor Andrew Young.

name: John W. E. Bowen
paragraphs: John Wesley Edward Bowen was known for his speaking ability and served as president of the Gammon Theological Seminary. He was a professor at major colleges like Howard University.
Bowen was the first African American to earn a PhD from Boston University and the second African American in the United States to earn a PhD.
During key periods like the 1906 Atlanta Race Riots, he risked his own safety to provide shelter for those affected by violence. He was unafraid to speak his mind on racial issues.
John Wesley Edward Bowen was a critical religious and intellectual leader in Atlanta. He lived in the city for many years and it became his final resting place.
Source: Wikipedia contributors, 'John W. E. Bowen Sr.'

name: Lillian Miles Lewis
paragraphs: Lillian Miles Lewis was an educator and political figure who supported her husband John Lewis's career while making her own lasting impact on Atlanta's schools through her work at Clark Atlanta University. Lillian Miles Lewis moved to Atlanta to work as a librarian at Atlanta University. She met her husband in 1967 and supported him when he ran for the Atlanta City Council and his 1986 congressional race. She impacted Atlanta's schools with her work at Clark Atlanta University.
Source: John and Lillian Miles Lewis Foundation
